CC would definitely like to be a high standard, but this goes to show what CC really is, which is a brilliant demonstration of the powers of targeted marketing: if CC represents a high standard, then that seems like something we want, but we'd still have to establish that CC really is a high standard. For one, if we're talking about good students, then it's not a high standard. This is a general truism - any common standard is not going to be a high standard when you're talking about good students. The downside is that CC is additionally a restrictive standard, because it puts unnecessary constraints on methodology when solving problems. As far as everyone else is concerned, though, it's still not clear that CC is a high standard. If the focus is on a method which is required rather than correctly arriving at a correct solution, then that's training following directions, not problem solving. It doesn't guarantee that students understand what they are doing or can generalize their approach.

Which brings us to the next point, how CC compares to foreign education. Once a person tried excusing CC by convincing me that it's really just the same way I learned math in school (for the sake of this discussion, I had a relatively good math education). Problem is, I did most of my learning on my own from foreign textbooks. Those books didn't really talk about method at all, they just had problems to solve. The key was in maintaining a sensible progression of difficulty. Even in school, the best teachers I had were big critics of teaching fads, meaning the idea that an education was defined by a bureaucratic standard rather than by the efforts of the teacher and the student.
I see Common Core as another Federal government over reach. This time to control the nations education system. States better wise up.
